title: Speaking practice: Compost, Discounts and Group Work
description: Eight speaking tasks: explain two discount methods, explain a puddle, argue from garden data, tell what happened to a class pet, record a message for a visiting science teacher, disagree politely, compare story endings and present island geography.

stimuli.title: Two ways to find a sale price
paragraphs: A jacket costs $40. The store takes 25% off the price. Two students found the sale price in different ways.
Student 1: “25% of 40 is 10. I subtract: 40 − 10 = 30.”
Student 2: “If 25% comes off, I still pay 75% of the price. 75% of 40 is 30.”
A classmate says: “The two methods are different, so the answers should be different.”

stimuli.title: Where did the puddle go?
paragraphs: On Monday morning, there was a big puddle on the school playground. The sun was shining all day. After lunch, the puddle was much smaller. By the end of the day, it was gone and the ground was dry.
Science note: Heat can turn liquid water into a gas called water vapor. This change is called evaporation.
A younger student asks you: “Where did the water go?”

stimuli.title: Does compost help tomato plants?
paragraphs: A school garden club tested whether compost helps tomato plants grow more fruit. In Bed A, they mixed compost into the soil around three plants. In Bed B, they planted three plants with no compost. All six plants got the same sunlight and the same water and were planted on the same day.
Tomatoes picked from each plant:
Bed A (with compost): 18, 21, 24
Bed B (no compost): 12, 15, 12
The club will present its results to the school.

stimuli.title: Why was Rosa late?
paragraphs: The class hamster, Pip, lives in a cage in Room 8. On Monday morning, the school custodian, Mr. Ortiz, found a problem. Here are his notes.
7:30 He opened the school and saw that the cage door was open and Pip was gone. He felt worried.
7:45 He heard a small noise in the hallway and followed the sound.
8:00 He found Pip asleep in a box of paper towels in the supply closet.
8:10 He carried Pip back to the cage and fixed the cage latch with a piece of wire.
8:30 The first students arrived, and Pip was safe.
Pretend you are Mr. Ortiz. The principal asks you what happened.

stimuli.title: A voice message for the substitute teacher
paragraphs: A visiting science teacher, Ms. Okoye, will take your class tomorrow. Your teacher asked you, as a lab helper, to record a voice message that explains how the science corner works. Here are your notes.
1. Goggles hang on the hooks by the sink. Put them on before you touch any liquid.
2. Each table has a tray with its materials. When you finish, put every item back on the tray.
3. If something spills, wipe it with the paper towels in the green box and tell the teacher.
4. To ask a question during an experiment, raise your hand and wait. Do not shout across the room.
5. In the last five minutes, wash your hands and answer the exit question at your seat.

stimuli.title: Disagree politely in a group
paragraphs: You are working in a group of three students on a model. You hear this conversation:
Sam: “I think we should each make a different part of the model alone and put them together on Friday. That way nobody has to wait.”
Lena: “I disagree. If we work separately, the parts might not fit together.”
Sam: “They will fit. You always want to control everything.”
Now the group is waiting for you to speak.

stimuli.title: Are surprise endings always better?
paragraphs: Two classmates disagree about stories.
Classmate 1 says: “A story is always better when it has a surprise ending.”
Classmate 2 says: “A surprise ending is good only if clues earlier in the story make it feel fair.”
Story 1: At the end, the narrator turns out to be a robot. Earlier in the story, the narrator never eats, never sleeps, and counts every step from the door to the bus.
Story 2: At the end, the last sentence says, “Then she woke up. It was all a dream.” Nothing earlier in the story suggested a dream.

stimuli.title: Present the geography of an island
paragraphs: Your class is designing a game about people settling on an island. A classmate needs to understand the island map before the game starts. Here is a description of the map.
North: tall mountains with snow in winter. A river begins here.
Middle: wide, flat plains with rich soil. The river flows through the plains.
East coast: a deep harbor where ships can anchor.
South: dry hills with few trees.
Distances: the harbor is about 6 kilometers from the plains and about 20 kilometers from the mountains.

items.stem: Explain each student's method to the classmate. Show why both methods give the same sale price, even though the methods look different.

checklist: I explained Student 1's steps.
I explained Student 2's steps.
I said why 100% minus 25% is 75%.
I stated the sale price.
I explained why the two methods give the same answer.
exemplar: Explains Student 1's method accurately (find the discount of $10, then subtract it from $40).
Explains Student 2's method accurately (the customer pays 100% − 25% = 75% of the price, and 75% of 40 is 30).
Connects the two methods and explains why they agree (taking 25% off leaves 75% to pay).
States the correct sale price, $30, with its unit, and uses accurate percent vocabulary.

support.clue: Ask: how much money comes off in Method 1? What part of the price is left in Method 2? Then connect the two ideas.
support.frame: Student 1 first finds ______, which is ______. Then the student ______, so the sale price is ______. Student 2 thinks about the part you still pay. Since ___% comes off, you pay ___% of the price, and ___% of 40 is ______. Both methods give the same answer because ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different situation): “A sunflower is 20 centimeters tall and grows 10% taller this week. Method 1 finds 10% of 20, which is 2, and adds: 20 + 2 = 22. Method 2 notices that the new height is 110% of the old height, and 110% of 20 is 22. Both methods give the same answer because adding 10% of the height makes 110% of the height.” Now explain the two methods for the jacket.

items.stem: Explain to the younger student why the puddle disappeared. Tell what happened to the water and what caused it.

checklist: I told what happened to the puddle.
I told what caused it.
I used the word because or so.
I used science words I know.
exemplar: Describes that the liquid water became a gas (water vapor) and went into the air.
Identifies the sun's heat as the cause.
Uses cause-and-effect language (because, so, as a result).
Uses scientific vocabulary such as evaporate, water vapor, or gas.
Speaks in clear sentences for a younger audience.

support.clue: Think about what the sun gives to the water, and what form the water changes into when it leaves the ground.
support.frame: The puddle disappeared because ______. First, ______. Then, the water ______. This happened because ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different situation): “The ice cream on the table turned into a puddle because the room was warm. First, the heat from the air reached the ice cream. Then, the ice cream melted into a liquid. This happened because warm air gives heat to cold things.” Now explain what happened to the puddle.

facts: Heat from the Sun causes liquid water to evaporate into water vapor, a gas, which goes into the air.

items.stem: Make a claim about whether compost helped the tomato plants. Support it with the average of each bed, explain your reasoning, and describe one limit of this evidence.

checklist: I stated a claim.
I used the average of each bed as evidence.
I explained why the evidence supports my claim.
I described one limit of the evidence.
I used science words such as compost, variable, or average.
exemplar: States a claim supported by the data (compost increased the number of tomatoes).
Calculates or states the averages accurately (Bed A 21 tomatoes per plant, Bed B 13 tomatoes per plant).
Explains the reasoning and notes that other conditions were kept the same.
Identifies a limit (only three plants in each bed; a larger sample or repeated trial would be stronger).
Uses claim, evidence, and reasoning structure and precise scientific language.

support.clue: Add the three numbers in each bed and divide by three. Then compare the two averages and think about how many plants were tested.
support.frame: My claim is that compost ______. The evidence is that the average for Bed A is ___ tomatoes, while the average for Bed B is ___ tomatoes. My reasoning is that the plants had the same ______, so the main difference was ______. However, one limit of this evidence is that ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different investigation): “My claim is that fertilizer helped the bean plants grow taller. The evidence is that the average height in Pot A was 30 centimeters, while the average in Pot B was 22 centimeters. My reasoning is that the plants had the same sunlight and water, so the main difference was the fertilizer. However, one limit of this evidence is that I measured only two plants in each pot.” Now make your claim about compost.

facts: The difference between the averages is 8 tomatoes per plant.

items.stem: Pretend you are Mr. Ortiz. Tell the principal what happened this morning in order, how you felt, and what you did so it will not happen again.

checklist: I told the events in order using I.
I used time words such as first, then, and after that.
I used past tense.
I told how I felt and what I did so it will not happen again.
exemplar: Tells all main events in the correct order from the custodian’s point of view (cage open, noise, finding Pip, fixing the latch).
Uses first-person pronouns consistently (I, my) and sequence and time expressions.
Uses past tense with mostly accurate control.
Names a feeling with a reason (worried because Pip was gone) and states the fix (the latch).
Speaks politely to the principal.

support.clue: Read the times down the list. For each time, say one sentence with I about what Mr. Ortiz did. Then find the moment he felt worried and the step that helps in the future.
support.frame: Good morning. I want to tell you what happened. First, I ______. Then I ______. After that, I ______. I felt ______ because ______. To keep it from happening again, I ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different story): “Last winter, I delivered the mail to a farm at the end of a long road. One morning, snow covered the road, so I could not drive. I felt worried because the family was waiting for a package. So I walked the last mile with the package in my arms. To keep the road clear, I called the town office.” Now tell the principal what happened as Mr. Ortiz.

items.stem: Record a message for the visiting science teacher. Present four science corner routines in a clear order and explain how each one helps the class.

checklist: I greeted the substitute and said the purpose of my message.
I explained four routines in a clear order.
I said how each routine helps the class.
I used order words and connecting words.
I ended with a polite closing.
exemplar: Opens with a greeting and a purpose statement.
Accurately presents four routines from the notes in a logical order.
Explains the purpose or benefit of each routine (for example, goggles protect eyes from liquid; the tray keeps materials organized; raising a hand keeps the room calm).
Uses transitions and discourse markers across the whole message.
Closes politely and speaks in a clear, appropriate register for an adult.

support.clue: Pick four notes. For each one, ask: what does this routine keep safe or make easier for the teacher or the class?
support.frame: Hello, Ms. Okoye, and welcome to our class. I will explain four routines. First, ______. This helps because ______. Second, ______. This helps the class ______. Third, ______. Finally, ______. Thank you for ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different place): “Hello, and welcome to swim practice. I will explain four routines. First, we walk on the pool deck. This helps because wet floors are slippery. Second, we hang our towels on the hooks. This helps the next group find space. Third, we stay in our own lane. Finally, we wait for the whistle before we start. Thank you for helping us.” Now give your message for the visiting science teacher.

items.stem: Respond to Sam and Lena. Disagree politely with Sam's last comment, give a reason for or against working separately, and suggest a plan that works for everyone.

checklist: I disagreed politely with Sam.
I gave a reason about working separately.
I suggested a plan.
I used polite words such as I understand, but, and maybe we could.
exemplar: Disagrees respectfully without blaming (focuses on the plan, not the person).
Gives a reason that fits the situation (parts may not fit; people need to share ideas).
Acknowledges a point from each speaker (Sam wants to avoid waiting, Lena worries about fit).
Proposes a workable compromise (share measurements first, work separately, then test the fit on Wednesday).
Uses polite, tactful language appropriate for peers.

support.clue: Find one good idea in what Sam said and one in what Lena said. Then think about a plan that keeps both.
support.frame: I understand that you want ______, Sam, but ______. Lena has a point because ______. I think working separately would ______ because ______. Maybe we could ______. That way, ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different disagreement): “I understand that you want to finish the video tonight, Ravi, but we are tired. Mia has a point because mistakes are easy to make late at night. I think rushing would hurt our video because we might forget scenes. Maybe we could record tonight and edit tomorrow. That way, we both finish on time and do good work.” Now respond to Sam and Lena.

items.stem: Decide which classmate you agree with more. Support your position with details from Story 1 and Story 2, and respond to one reason from the other side.

checklist: I stated which classmate I agree with more.
I used details from both stories.
I compared the two endings.
I answered one reason from the other side.
I used a word such as although, however, or on the other hand.
exemplar: States a clear position that responds to both classmates' ideas.
Uses specific details from both stories (the narrator's habits as clues; the dream ending with no clues).
Compares the two endings using criteria such as fairness, clues, and whether the ending feels earned.
Acknowledges a counterargument (a surprise can be exciting) and responds to it.
Uses complex sentences with contrast connectors and literary vocabulary such as foreshadowing, clues, and ending.

support.clue: Compare what the reader knew before the ending in Story 1 and Story 2. Ask which ending felt prepared and which felt sudden.
support.frame: I agree more with Classmate ___ because ______. In Story 1, ______, which shows ______. In Story 2, ______. Classmate ___ might say ______. However, ______. For these reasons, ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different topic): “I agree more with Coach Dara's rule that every player should rest for one game each week, because it prevents injuries. In Team 1, the players who rested stayed healthy all season. In Team 2, nobody rested and three players were hurt. Some people might say that resting makes the team weaker. However, an injured player cannot play at all. For these reasons, rest helps the team.” Now give your position on surprise endings.

items.stem: Present the island's geography to the new settlers. Describe at least four places, say how each place could be useful or difficult for settlers, and organize your talk in a clear order.

checklist: I described at least four places.
I told how each place could help or challenge settlers.
I used place words such as north, middle, east, and south.
I used a clear order.
exemplar: Accurately describes at least four places using the map details.
Explains a likely use or difficulty for each (rivers give fresh water; plains are good for farming; a deep harbor allows ships; dry hills are hard for growing crops).
Uses geographic vocabulary (plains, harbor, mountains, river) and direction words.
Organizes the talk in a clear sequence such as north to south, with an opening and closing.
Uses noun groups for detailed description (tall mountains with snow, wide flat plains).

support.clue: Go place by place. For each one, ask: what could people do there, and what could be hard?
support.frame: The island has ______ in the north. A river begins there, so ______. In the middle, there are ______, which are good for ______ because ______. On the east coast, there is ______, so ______. In the south, there are ______. They could be difficult because ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different place): “The valley has a lake in the west. Fish live there, so people can catch food. In the center, there are thick forests, which are good for building houses because trees give wood. In the east, there is a narrow canyon, so travel is slow. In the south, there is a wide road, which makes it easier to bring supplies.” Now present the island to the settlers.

facts: Flat land with rich soil is good for farming.
A deep harbor lets ships anchor.
Mountains with snow can feed rivers with meltwater.
Dry land with few trees is difficult for growing crops.
